newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Empire Blue Cross exec convicted of perjury.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Empire Blue Cross exec convicted of perjury.

text.p: The former top financial officer of Empire Blue Cross Blue Shield, a major non-profit health insurer, was convicted Monday of perjury and obstructing a U.S. Senate subcommittee investigation.

Jerry Weissman of Brooklyn was convicted by a Manhattan federal jury on three of four counts accusing him of lying about data that exaggerated losses Empire suffered from insuring high-risk clients. The jury could not reach an agreement on one of the perjury counts.
He faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine on each of the three counts.

Weissman and two actuaries who worked with him were fired by Empire in July 1993 for their alleged role in a scheme to destroy financial documents and file false data with the New York State Insurance Department.
The firings stemmed from a scandal that engulfed Empire relating to disclosures about management failures and financial discrepancies.

Empire had argued for years that the state unfairly forced it to serve high-risk clients -- the oldest and sickest of New York residents -- while its for-profit competitors did not have to offer coverage to everyone.
The insurer had used false data to lobby the New York legislature, which in 1992 passed a law requiring for-profit insurers to offer plans to all individuals and small groups.

The majority of Empire's business is broken into two segments: "community rated" for individuals, families and small businesses, and "experience rated" for large companies. The community rated segment is regulated by New York State.
The indictment alleged Weissman was part of a scheme between 1989 and 1992 to give the state financial reports on these segments that differed from internal findings.

The reports filed with the state allegedly showed worse results from the community segment and better results from the experience segment than the internal report. The indictment alleged that Weissman designed different formats for the reports to conceal the discrepancies from the state.

In August 1992, the New York State legislature passed a law requiring an independent audit of Empire. Weissman then allegedly met with subordinates in the actuarial department who were involved in creating the false figures and told them they had to come up with an explanation for the discrepancies.
The same year the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations of the Committee of Governmental Affairs began a probe of Empire.
The indictment alleged that Weissman gave the subcommittee and an independent auditor false information to back up the state reports.
He was also charged with lying in 1993 testimony before the subcommittee.
